turns.t: Hi, doctor, sorry, I'm a little out of breath, I took the stairs because the elevator was packed with a whole group of kids on some field trip.
No problem, have a seat. You're here for the follow-up on the racing heart episodes. How have they been since I saw you last?
Better, honestly. Not gone, but better. I still get the racing heart, like my chest is a drum solo, maybe twice a week now instead of every day.
Twice a week. And what's usually going on when it starts?
Well, it's funny you ask, because on Monday it hit me in the cereal aisle at the grocery store. Of all places. A guy was stacking boxes right behind me and I just thought, here we go.
Does it tend to be crowds, or noise?
Crowded subway cars are the worst. I took a different train all last month just to avoid the rush, which added forty minutes, and my husband said I was being ridiculous, but it worked.
Okay. How long does one of these last?
Ten minutes, give or take. Then I'm wiped out, like I ran a marathon. I teach fifth grade, so you can imagine how that goes when it happens at recess.
Let's go through your medicines so I have the list right. What are you taking at the moment?
The sertraline, 50 milligrams, once a day in the morning. The propranolol, ten milligrams, only when I feel one coming on. And the lisinopril for my blood pressure, ten milligrams every morning.
Good. Any chest pain with the episodes, or have you passed out at all?
No chest pain. And no fainting, I've never actually fainted, I just feel like the floor is tilting a little.
Fine. Any other conditions I should have on file besides the blood pressure?
Just the panic disorder, which you know about. My mother always says I get it from worrying, but I told her it's not that simple.
She's right that stress doesn't help, but it's more than worry. Let me get your numbers. Arm out for me.
Blood pressure is 126 over 78. Pulse is 72 and regular.
Is that good? My pulse was ninety at the dentist last week, but he was holding a drill.
That's good. Oxygen saturation is 98 percent, breathing rate is 14 a minute, and your weight is 142 pounds.
A pound up from March. I blame the banana bread phase.
Nothing alarming in that. Let me listen to your heart and lungs now, lean forward a little.
Doctor, just so you know, the monitor kit is charged and sitting in room two if you need it.
Thanks, I might. Deep breath in for me... and out.
Heart sounds are normal, regular rhythm, and no murmur that I can hear. Lungs are clear.
So my heart is okay? Because when it races I really do think it's going to stop.
I understand that fear. Right now, this still looks most likely like panic attacks rather than a rhythm problem. But because you describe it so vividly, I'd like to be sure.
Sure how? Another ECG? I had one at a walk-in clinic and they said it was fine, but my car mechanic says everything is fine too, right before it breaks down.
Fair point. I'm going to arrange a twenty-four hour heart monitor so we catch an actual episode on tape, and I'd like to order a thyroid blood test, since an overactive thyroid can mimic this.
Oh, a blood test, that's easy. I just hate when they ask me to make a fist and pump it.
Right. The monitor goes on today, you wear it for a day, bring it back tomorrow. Keep a note of the time if you feel anything.
Can I shower with it on?
No, keep it dry. Sponge bath for a day.
My students will say I smell like marker anyway. Okay.
On the sertraline, keep going exactly as you are, and keep using the propranolol only as you've been doing. No changes today.
Great. I was afraid you'd take something away.
Not at all. Try slow breathing in those first couple of minutes, in for four, out for six. It actually works on the heart rate.
I've been practicing it in the cereal aisle. Maybe I should practice it more before the cereal aisle.
That's the idea. I'd like to see you again in six weeks, with the results in hand.
Six weeks, that works, that's right after the spring break.
Hi, I can book that six-week visit at the front desk whenever you're ready, and the kit tech will meet you in the corridor.
Perfect. Thank you, doctor. Give my regards to the rest of the clinic, and your new haircut looks great, by the way.
Ha, thank you. Take care.

medications.name: propranolol
medications.frequency: only when I feel one coming on

clinical_actions.description: Slow breathing technique at onset of episodes
